extracted.intended_audience: patent scholars, patent lawyers, judges, and law students interested in claim construction theory
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical and doctrinal framework for distinguishing the linguistic interpretation of patent claim text from the normative construction of its legal effect; explains when linguistic tools can resolve disputes and when policy-based construction is required. Applied to patent claim analysis and case law debates (e.g., Phillips, Markman, Phillips-era disputes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation (discern linguistic meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation is the process of discerning the linguistic meaning of a text using linguistic tools: the set of ideas and concepts that are communicated by the language to a member of the intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation is factual and objective (what the text communicates to its intended audience); it uses linguistic evidence (usage patterns, dictionaries, grammar, context) and is distinct from normative considerations. Interpretation usually can resolve apparent ambiguities when sufficient contextual evidence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction (determine legal meaning/effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction is the activity of determining the legal meaning and effect of a text; the legal meaning may or may not track the linguistic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction is irreducibly normative and involves policy judgments and legal principles (textualism, utilitarianism, deontology, etc.). It includes deciding whether courts should follow linguistic meaning or tailor legal scope (e.g., to the real invention). Construction addresses the questions that remain after interpretation, especially when linguistic meaning underdetermines legal outcomes (the 'construction zone').

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation–Construction Distinction (conceptual tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interpretation-construction distinction separates determining linguistic meaning (interpretation) from giving legal effect (construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to identify whether a dispute is about semantic meaning (solvable by linguistic evidence) or about normative legal effect (requires policy arguments). Avoid conflating the two: many claim disputes presented as linguistic are actually normative construction disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent Ambiguity: resolve by interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent ambiguity arises when text seems to support more than one linguistic sense but, properly interpreted, normally has a single correct linguistic meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve apparent ambiguity by looking to context, grammar, surrounding text, and conventional usage (example: Merrill v. Yeomans—'manufacture' resolved to mean process in context). If adequate contextual evidence exists, interpretation will produce a determinate answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness (open texture) requires construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Vagueness occurs when a term has fuzzy boundaries (borderline cases) and cannot be made determinate by linguistic tools alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because vagueness leaves borderline cases, linguistic investigation cannot resolve legal outcomes for those cases; construction (policy-based decisionmaking) is required to fill the gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction Zone (when linguistic meaning underdetermines legal effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'construction zone' is the space where linguistic information underdetermines legal effect—where interpretation does not yield a sufficiently determinate legal outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a dispute falls inside the construction zone; if so, solutions must be normatively justified rather than framed as purely linguistic fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation is evidence-dependent (availability of linguistic evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The success of interpretation depends on the availability and quality of contextual and historical linguistic evidence (usage patterns, dictionaries, translators, expert interpreters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evidence (intrinsic or extrinsic) is lacking, interpretative questions may remain unresolved; but that is an epistemic gap, not a denial of objective linguistic meaning. Examples: unfamiliar historical usage (Shakespeare) or technical jargon in patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intrinsic evidence (specification, whole patent context) in interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent specification and the remainder of the patent document are relevant contextual evidence for discerning linguistic meaning of claim terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual reading of claims with the specification (e.g., subject-matter focus, grammar, how terms are used elsewhere in the patent) often resolves ambiguities; but this is an inquiry about ordinary linguistic usage rather than an argument that claims must be read to match the patentee's inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony, translators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries, encyclopedias, expert testimony, technical translators and other extrinsic sources can be used as proxies to determine how the intended audience would understand claim language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence is appropriate for unfamiliar languages or technical jargon; such sources are proxies for usage patterns and the understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art. But extrinsic evidence is secondary to intrinsic evidence when intrinsic context is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity versus Vagueness (distinction and diagnostic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity: a term has more than one sense. Vagueness: a term has fuzzy, borderline cases. These are distinct problems with different remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent ambiguity is generally resolvable by interpretation (context, grammar, usage). Vagueness cannot be eliminated by linguistic tools and thus requires construction (policy choices about borderline cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain and ordinary meaning / dictionary definitions as interpretive tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts and commentators often appeal to 'plain meaning' or dictionary definitions to determine claim term meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictionaries can provide evidence of conventional meaning but are proxies for deeper linguistic usage; overreliance or overstatement of 'plainness' may mischaracterize disputes that are actually normative. Use dictionaries as one piece of evidence, not the sole determinant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of Ordinary Skill in the Art (POSITA) as interpretive audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation often seeks the understanding that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have of claim terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony and technical evidence help establish this audience's understanding; patent claims are written for POSITA, so their conventions and jargon matter in discerning linguistic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention-centered (anti-textualist/pragmatic) vs text-centered (textualist) approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Competing normative theories of construction: some argue claims should be construed according to the patentee's actual invention (invention-centered / anti-textualist / pragmatic textualism), while others argue for fidelity to the claim text (textualism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this as a policy disagreement about what legal effect claim language should have; choosing between them is a constructional decision, not purely interpretive. Each approach carries different implications for patent scope and judicial role.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple linguistic meanings are intentionally conveyed (double meanings/gibberish), treat as construction
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author intentionally conveys multiple linguistic meanings (double entendre) or the text is gibberish (no coherent linguistic meaning), there is no single correct linguistic interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such situations are exceptional; when multiple intended meanings exist, courts must resort to constructional tools (policy, purposive arguments) to determine legal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional allocation for claim analysis (who decides and why)
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether appellate judges, district judges, juries, specialized trial courts, or the PTO are best positioned to perform claim analysis and implement chosen interpretive or constructional methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for allocation hinge on which actor is better equipped to analyze written documents, technical evidence, or policy tradeoffs. Recognize that institutional allocation is often premised on the belief that the root problem is linguistic; if the problem is constructional, institutional arguments shift to who should make normative policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish construction from application (legal scope vs fact application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction determines, as a matter of law, what the patentee's legal monopoly covers; application is the subsequent step of comparing an accused product to that legal scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should construe claims (legal meaning) before applying that construction to the facts. But the fact that a court chooses a particular legal scope does not prove that this is the linguistic meaning of the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation is objective and resists radical indeterminacy claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The linguistic meanings of legal texts are not radically indeterminate; linguistic communication works, and interpretation yields objective answers when evidence is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject the Critical Legal Studies-style claim that 'law means whatever judges say'; interpretative questions are factual in nature even if hard in practice. Empirical indicators like reversal rates do not in themselves prove semantic indeterminacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of grammar and ordinary usage conventions in resolving meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar and ordinary rules of usage (including reading the claim in the context of surrounding sentences) are valid interpretive tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply grammatical analysis and ordinary-language reading to discern which sense of an ambiguous term fits the claim context (example: identifying 'manufacture' as a process in Merrill v. Yeomans).

rubrics_metrics.name: When interpretive evidence is missing, uncertainty persists (epistemic limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if linguistic meaning objectively exists, courts may be unable to discern it because of lack of evidence (historical record, technical usage data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the epistemic limits: absence of evidence yields unresolved interpretative questions, which may then require constructional (policy) responses or further evidentiary investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy theories as competing constructional criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructional choices should be guided by an explicit theory of what legal outcomes aim to achieve (e.g., maximize economic efficiency, adhere to moral principles, preserve textual fidelity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make policy arguments explicit when operating in the construction zone; evaluate proposed constructions as policy proposals rather than as purportedly better linguistic interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-textualist caution: do not conflate linguistic context with the patentee's inventive contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the specification as linguistic context (to discern ordinary usage) differs from the anti-textualist move that interprets claims according to the patentee's inventive contribution or what the patentee 'justly' has a right to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reasoning that because the inventor only conceived certain embodiments the claim must be limited to them; that is a constructional/invention-centered normative move, not a purely interpretive one.
